# Latrines and sewers (keeping excrement out of water, food and soil) (`sanitation_sewerage`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, cholera_waterborne, public_health_board, fired_brick_ceramics
- Core idea: Most deadly diarrhoeal diseases and worms travel from one person's excrement to another's mouth through water, hands, flies, soil and crops. Every household needs a pit latrine: a pit two or three metres deep whose bottom stays at least 1.5 m above the groundwater, about 30 m from any well and downhill of it, with a slab, a tight lid or a vent pipe against flies, and a place to wash hands next to it. Cover a full pit with earth and dig a new one. Night soil for the fields must undergo treatment verified to destroy persistent worm eggs. In towns, closed sewers must carry waste to a point downstream of every water intake; a water-seal bend (S-trap) under each drain keeps the gas and the rats out of the house.
- Pitfalls:
  - Building sewers that empty into the river above the water intake; London's cholera got worse after cesspools were flushed into the Thames in the 1840s
  - Digging the latrine next to or uphill of the well, or down to the groundwater
  - Fighting the smell (perfume, lime on top, burning herbs) instead of the contact with excrement
  - Spreading fresh night soil on vegetables; roundworm eggs survive for months
  - Assuming Roman-style baths and public latrines made people healthy; shared sponges and warm unchanged bath water did not, and Roman-era remains show as many intestinal parasites as before
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3000–2500 BC – clay drain pipes and brick-lined latrines over cesspits (e.g. Eshnunna); india: c. 2600–1900 BC – Indus cities (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa): house latrines and bathrooms connected to covered brick street drains; greece: c. 1700 BC – Minoan Knossos: stone drains and a latrine flushed with water; rome: c. 6th c. BC – Cloaca Maxima begun as a drainage channel (traditional date); imperial public latrines and sewers, mainly for drainage and convenience; china: Han period (206 BC – AD 220) – latrines built over pigsties; organised collection of night soil as fertiliser in later cities; europe: 1596 – Harington's flushing closet; 1775 Cumming patents the S-trap; 1842 Chadwick's sanitary report; 1859–1875 Bazalgette's intercepting sewers for London
- Read:
  - Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain (1842)
  - E. G. Wagner and J. N. Lanoix, Excreta Disposal for Rural Areas and Small Communities (World Health Organization, 1958)
  - Stephen Halliday, The Great Stink of London (1999)
